title: Leadership
author: Empathy Elevated
summary: This article describes a pattern common to high-performing contributors: the gap between competence as measured by outputs and perception as measured by how one handles the high-pressure process of producing those outputs. The central insight is that under conditions of urgency and stress, competent people tend to shift into intense problem-solving mode, narrowing attention and dropping relational signals, while the people around them experience these behavioral shifts as negative leadership cues. The author argues that intent does not transmit; signal does: it does not matter that the contributor was doing the right thing internally if the external signals emitted during that process were read as disengagement or lack of care. The practical implication is a form of dual-channel management: maintaining technical throughput while also managing the relational signal the team and stakeholders are reading in real time. The cost arrives late, well after the work is delivered, in the form of relationships and reputations that have quietly changed.
points: Competence is evaluated upon delivery; perception is evaluated in real time, and by the time the work is delivered the room has already formed impressions that the quality of the output may not be able to reverse.

High-pressure moments are exactly when most people are least able to manage their external signals: the cognitive resources required by intense problem-solving are the same ones available for social calibration, and they cannot fully serve both simultaneously.
The intent-does-not-transmit; signal-does principle shifts responsibility from recipient to sender: the contributor is responsible for signals emitted regardless of internal state.

People around a stressed high-performer often lose their empathy for that person, experiencing the behavioral effects of the colleague's stress without access to the internal experience and filling the interpretive gap with negative readings.
The skill this article describes is deliberate signal management: maintaining enough awareness of how one's behavior reads to others during stress to preserve the relational fabric the team needs.

Solving a problem rapidly with little support, and the team relying on you with your track record of competence.

The high-pressure moments are the ones where you are most likely to produce a read you didn't intend. If you are under severe stress, the time for niceties goes out the window. Others might not be on the same page, or even if they agree in theory, they still get hurt by the perceived lack of care in practice.

They are enduring your stress and feeling your stress. The completion of reaching the deadline feels irrelevant. People walk away with a negative impression you did not intend, not remembering the sacrifice of the hard work you put in to complete the task at hand.

It's easy for this to go out the window when you are trying to reach a deadline. But what good is reaching the deadline if those around you are pissed at you at the end, because of your "attitude" or "lack of listening"? But the work lands in a room full of people who remember how it felt to be in it with you.
